  • The twisted pedicle is the most specific CT sign but is reported in fewer than one third of cases; multiplanar reformations help.
  • Heterogeneous, minimal, or absent enhancement supports progression toward infarction/necrosis; noncontrast hematoma or hematosalpinx may exceed 50 HU.
MR Imaging
  • T1-weighted: stromal edema is low signal; T1 hyperintensity supports hemorrhage/hemorrhagic infarction or hematosalpinx.
  • T2-weighted: edematous stroma is high signal with peripheral hyperintense follicles; dark tissue may indicate infarcted/nonviable tissue.
  • Absent stromal enhancement supports infarction; MRI can also depict the twisted pedicle and abnormal ovarian position.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Hemorrhagic corpus luteum/cyst: common false positive; favor an otherwise normal ovary with preserved vascularity and reticular/fishnet fibrin, retractile clot, fluid-fluid/debris level, or rim flow.
  • Ectopic pregnancy: positive beta-hCG, absent intrauterine pregnancy, tubal ring/ring of fire, adnexal mass separate from ovary, embryo/yolk sac when visible, or hemoperitoneum if ruptured.
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease: thickened/dilated tubes, pyosalpinx, hyperemia, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, or complex inflammatory adnexal mass.
  • Isolated fallopian tube torsion: abnormal thick-walled/dilated tube with normal ovaries; a whirlpool sign may still be present.

⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Normal arterial or even venous flow does not exclude acute or incomplete torsion.
  • Preserved central venous flow can favor viability; absent ovarian/pedicle flow or absent enhancement increases concern for necrosis/infarction.
  • Adult torsion often has a benign lead point such as a physiologic/corpus luteum cyst, dermoid, paraovarian cyst, or other benign mass.
  • Pregnancy may displace the ovary far cephalad; neonatal torsion can present as an abdominal mass.

🚩 Board-Relevant Pivots
  • The twisted vascular pedicle is the direct mechanical sign; when identified it is highly specific/pathognomonic.
  • Do not use Doppler as a binary gatekeeper: morphology plus position plus pedicle remain decisive.
  • Treatment is urgent surgery, with detorsion when viable and salpingo-oophorectomy when necrotic/infarcted; address a lead-point mass.

⭐ Super Summary
  • Think: enlarged edematous displaced ovary → peripheral follicles → variable Doppler → search for twisted pedicle → assess hemorrhage/nonenhancement/necrosis and a lead point.

🧭 Adnexal/Ovarian Torsion
Adnexal torsion is rotation of the ovary/adnexa on its vascular pedicle, producing venous and lymphatic congestion before arterial compromise, with possible hemorrhagic infarction and necrosis. Imaging diagnosis rests on ovarian morphology and position, vascular assessment, and deliberate search for the twisted pedicle.

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core Radiology GU p. 315 supplies the board-level torsion framework; RadPrimer provides the canonical article backbone and image set; STATdx supplies Doppler, viability, CT/MR, pediatric, and lead-point depth.

📌 Abbreviations / Acronyms
  • US = ultrasound
  • CECT = contrast-enhanced CT
  • MR = magnetic resonance

🔍 Summary
  • Adnexal torsion is the more precise term because the tube commonly twists with the ovary; isolated tubal torsion can occur.
  • Vascular sequence: venous and lymphatic obstruction precede arterial compromise; prolonged compromise can progress to ischemia, hemorrhagic infarction, and necrosis.
  • Classic clinical setting is sudden severe pelvic pain with nausea/vomiting; intermittent torsion-detorsion can produce episodic pain.
